lesson.title: Counting ATP: Why the Old Textbook Number Was Wrong
lesson.summary: Cellular respiration yields approximately 30 to 32 ATP per glucose molecule under typical conditions, a modern, more accurate revision of the older 36 to 38 ATP figure that assumed fixed, idealized conversion ratios.
lesson.body:
Adding up the total ATP yield of cellular respiration means combining three separate sources covered across this chapter: substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation driven by the NADH and FADH2 those pathways generate. Glycolysis nets 2 ATP directly. The Krebs cycle, running twice per glucose, nets 2 more ATP or GTP directly. That leaves 4 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation alone, a fixed number that does not depend on any assumptions about the electron transport chain.

The much larger and more variable contribution comes from oxidative phosphorylation, converting the 10 NADH and 2 FADH2 produced across glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle. Older textbooks assumed a clean, fixed ratio of 3 ATP per NADH and 2 ATP per FADH2, which is where the classic 36 to 38 ATP total came from. More careful measurements of the actual number of protons pumped per electron pair, and the actual number of protons ATP synthase needs to make one ATP, show that the true ratios are lower and not perfectly whole numbers, closer to about 2.5 ATP per NADH and about 1.5 ATP per FADH2. Using those more accurate ratios brings the oxidative phosphorylation contribution down substantially from the old estimate.

There is a further complication specific to the 2 NADH produced by glycolysis in the cytoplasm, since NADH itself cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly and must be shuttled in. Which shuttle a particular cell uses changes the final number. Heart, liver, and kidney cells generally use the malate-aspartate shuttle, which transfers the electrons with essentially no loss, so those cytoplasmic NADH still yield about 2.5 ATP each once inside. Skeletal muscle and brain cells more often use the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle, which hands the electrons to FAD-linked carriers already inside the membrane rather than to NAD+, costing some energy in the transfer and yielding closer to 1.5 ATP each.

Putting the pieces together under typical, malate-aspartate-shuttle conditions: 4 ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation, plus roughly 2.5 ATP times 10 NADH, plus roughly 1.5 ATP times 2 FADH2, works out to approximately 32 ATP per glucose. Under glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle conditions the total comes out closer to 30 ATP. This is why modern sources generally cite a range of approximately 30 to 32 ATP per glucose rather than a single fixed number.

It is honest to flag that even this revised range is an approximation, not a precisely fixed constant. The exact yield depends on which shuttle mechanism a given cell type uses, on how tightly coupled electron transport and ATP synthesis are in that mitochondrion, on proton leak across the inner membrane, and on how much of the proton gradient gets diverted to other mitochondrial work, such as transporting ATP itself out to the rest of the cell. Biochemists still debate the precise figures, and different sources will list numbers that vary by a point or two within that same 30 to 32 range. The larger, more important takeaway for understanding respiration is not memorizing a single exact number, it is recognizing why oxidative phosphorylation so dramatically outproduces substrate-level phosphorylation, and why the presence or absence of oxygen makes such an enormous difference to how much usable energy a cell can extract from one glucose molecule.
